He reports slight chest cramps that seem to go away about an hour or so after he first feels them. He reports a slight cough and is not sure if it is due to the change of seasons and getting a cold. Regarding heart failure, he reports he has generally been pretty good about healthy food intake ever since, though the last year has been chaotic and he wanted to make sure he stayed on top of it. Russell reports several days of sharp pain on the right side of the abdomen below the ribs. The pain radiates to the lower abdomen and groin. It is intermittent and severe when it occurs, and he is unable to find a comfortable position. He reports burning with urination and occasionally dark urine, without frank blood. He has taken Tylenol without relief. He reports nausea but no vomiting, fever, or chills. He has a family history of kidney stones in his father. Gastrointestinal: Right-sided abdominal pain radiating to lower abdomen and groin; nausea.
Genitourinary: Burning with urination; occasionally dark urine; no frank blood noted.

Assessment: Acute nephrolithiasis, with a 0.5 cm stone in the proximal right ureter.

- Order basic metabolic panel, urinalysis, and urine culture.
- Follow up in 1 to 2 weeks. If symptoms persist, discuss further treatment such as lithotripsy or ureteroscopy.
- Contact provider if symptoms worsen.

Worsening headaches over the past few months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Bruce Ward is a 52-year-old male with a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion, seen in consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard for possible surgical intervention. He presented to his primary care provider, Dr. Howard, on 3/1/21 with worsening headaches over the past few months. He denied any prior headache problems. His past clinical history is unremarkable. Workup for worsening headaches was initiated with brain MRI and serology, and a pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered. The patient reports headaches located behind the eyes, described as a dull nagging ache. Onset was gradual about three months ago, and they have worsened over time from 3/10 to 6/10 severity. Headaches tend to be worse in the morning, last a few hours at a time, and nothing makes them better or worse. He notes recently bumping into door frames. He denies nausea, fever, rash, neck issues, numbness, tingling, weakness, or passing out. He denies change in vision or balance; his eyes were checked in the fall. He has no medical problems and takes no medicines. He tried Tylenol a few times for headaches without effect and stopped. Family history is unknown because he was adopted. He works as a computer programmer, has been married for 25 years, and recently bought a small house. He denies alcohol, smoking, or recreational drug use.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever or feeling sick. Neurologic: Denies numbness, tingling, weakness, neck stiffness, or passing out; reports bumping into door frames. Denies visual changes or balance problems. Skin: Denies rash. No nausea.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patient is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent. Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity and eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

RESULTS
Labs dated 3/3/21, including CBC, UNEs, coagulation, and CRP, were normal. Pituitary hormone profile showed low TSH; all other results were normal. MRI of the brain with contrast dated 3/4/21 revealed a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles were normal in size, and no other abnormalities were noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diagnosis: Pituitary adenoma. Bruce Ward is a 52-year-old male with a benign-appearing pituitary adenoma incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches. He is symptomatic with clinical and radiographic evidence of optic chiasmal compression; therefore, surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated. The mass appears benign, but diagnosis cannot be confirmed without sending the removed adenoma to pathology.
